title: Should You Buy Amazon Stock Now or Wait for a Dip?
detail:
Should You Buy Amazon Stock Now or Wait for a Dip?
David Jagielski, CPA, The Motley Fool
Mon, October 26, 2026 at 3:58 PM EDT 3 min read
AMZN
NVDA
^GSPC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

For not only years, but decades, Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) has been a top growth stock to buy and hold. It's generated massive returns for investors. But lately, that just hasn't been the case. In the past 12 months, it's up by just 11%. While that's a decent return, it trails the S&P 500, which has risen by 13% during that time frame.

There's been a lack of excitement around the stock of late, and it's down 6% in the past six months. Should investors buy it right now, or hold off for an even greater dip in price before doing so?

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Amazon.

This is not typical territory for Amazon stock to be in

In the past, it wasn't uncommon for Amazon's stock to trade at inflated multiples with respect to earnings. Paying more than 50 or 60 times earnings wasn't unheard of, given how much growth potential the company had. Today, however, it's trading at a price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple of just 20. And while it did get a boost from investment-related gains in its most recent results, even on a forward earnings basis, which factors in analyst expectations, its forward P/E multiple is still fairly low at 23.

Meanwhile, the company has continued to do well. When it released its second-quarter results in July, its sales were up a solid 20% and operating income was even more impressive, rising by 43% year over year. The growth hasn't dried up by any means. Meanwhile, the business still has plenty of opportunities for growth related to artificial intelligence (AI), which should lead to even better results in the future.

Investors may be less excited about the business due to the flurry of other AI stocks to choose from.

Has Amazon's stock become a bargain buy?

In five years, Amazon's stock has risen a relatively modest 47%. That includes, however, the crash that took place in 2022. With the company a leader in tech and AI innovation, it can make for a tremendous long-term buy, particularly given its reduced valuation.

While the stock may potentially go lower if there are concerns related to the tech sector as a whole and inflated levels of capital spending on AI, Amazon remains one of the best tech stocks to buy. Investors shouldn't assume a greater decline is coming for Amazon's stock, as it already looks like a great buy right now, and a rally may be overdue.

title: Anthropic’s IPO Will “Suck a Massive Amount of Money” From AI Stocks, Cramer Warns

Anthropic's IPO Will "Suck a Massive Amount of Money" From AI Stocks, Cramer Warns ©TIKR
Key Takeaways

Meta Platforms launched $35 billion of stock offerings on Monday and plans a separate $60 billion program in 2027, on the same day Anthropic reportedly planned to file publicly for its IPO.

Jim Cramer warns that Anthropic's listing will pull money away from the rest of the AI group, a group that includes Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet.

Nvidia's forward P/E is at 17x, the low of its three-year range, even though analysts' estimate of its fiscal 2028 earnings has risen 25% since the end of June.

Microsoft looks the most exposed: it trades at 27x forward earnings, and its three-year low is 19x.

AI investors are about to be asked for a lot more money.

On Monday, Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) launched $35 billion of stock offerings. That same morning, Anthropic planned to make its IPO filing public, Bloomberg reported. The Claude maker reportedly expects its IPO to match or beat the size of SpaceX's.

Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) wants a piece of Meta's deal too. It's one of three chipmakers that said they might buy up to $5 billion of Meta's new shares, though none of them has committed.

Jim Cramer saw this problem coming. On Mad Money a week ago, he warned that Anthropic's listing will "suck a massive amount of money away from the rest of the group" just because Anthropic is so big.

That group includes Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ), Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ) and Alphabet (GOOG), and all three report earnings this week.

And Meta is just getting started.

Meta's share count is headed the other way

For years, Meta has been shrinking its diluted share count. It fell about 10% from fiscal 2021 to fiscal 2025, to 2.57 billion.

Meta Platforms (META): diluted shares outstanding, billions of shares, fiscal 2021–2025 (TIKR)

Now Meta is adding stock. The new deals are $22.5 billion of Class A shares and about $12.5 billion of mandatory convertible preferred stock, with a separate $60 billion at-the-market program planned for 2027. Meta expects $135 billion to $145 billion of capex this year. It plans to pay for that with operating cash flow, investment-grade debt, partnerships and new stock.

Daniel Niles, a veteran tech investor, pointed out on X that Meta said in a recent filing that everyone is competing for the same pool of money. In his view, that pool "no longer seems endless like it did back earlier in the year."

title: Brazil markets battered after Lula win, AI in focus elsewhere
detail:
Brazil markets battered after Lula win, AI in focus elsewhere
AFP
Mon, October 26, 2026 at 4:16 PM EDT 4 min read
Anthropic's stock market listing will test investor appetite to continue funding AI development (ANDREJ IVANOV)

Brazilian markets took a battering Monday following the shock reelection of leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, but elsewhere investors were focused on artificial intelligence (AI) technology companies.

Lula came from behind to win in the second-round vote, but his right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of jailed ex-leader Jair Bolsonaro, has vowed to challenge the result.

Brazilian markets reeled as trading got under way, but pared some of the steepest losses by the close. The Sao Paulo stock exchange plummeted by 13.7 percent to near a two-month low, with the real down around 8.5 percent against the dollar.

"Instead of fiscal consolidation under Bolsonaro, Brazilian assets are instead going to have to contend with Lula's campaign pledges, including a shorter working week," said Chris Turner at ING bank.

Elsewhere, investors geared up for the week's crucial run of central bank decisions and tech earnings for major companies.

"The AI complex remains under a microscope ahead of what may be the most important stretch of earnings season so far," noted SPI Asset Management's Stephen Innes.

"Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon are about to walk on stage, and this is not one of those quarters where a company can simply beat the number, raise the guidance by a whisker and expect applause. Investors want proof now.

"They want to know whether the billions going into the compute buildout are building a durable earnings machine or just a shinier version of the same old capex furnace," Innes added.

This week also sees the release of earnings from South Korean chipmakers SK hynix and Samsung.

- Testing investor appetite -

Results from Tesla and Meta last week stoked spending worries that weighed on stock markets.

Nevertheless, Meta announced Monday it was launching a stock offering that aims to raise $35 billion to fund its AI ambitions.

The parent company of Facebook and Instagram also announced plans to launch an additional stock offering of up to $60 billion, at a date yet to be determined.

Meta's shares fell by 1.88 percent at the close.

Anthropic, one of the world's leading artificial intelligence companies, on Monday made public its plans to sell shares on the stock market in mid-November.

The company reported first-half revenue up about 1,300 percent year-over-year, but also flagged safety risks.

Wall Street's main indices closed higher on Monday, with the tech-rich Nasdaq gaining 0.8 percent.

"Tech is once again mounting an attempt to rally, like a battered prize fighter getting up off the floor," said Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at online trading and investing platform IG.

Instacart, valued at about $12 billion before the reports, has faced slowing growth since its 2023 IPO amid competition from DoorDash, Uber and Amazon.

A combination would unite two major players in food and grocery delivery but could face significant antitrust scrutiny given their overlapping businesses. DoorDash and Instacart held acquisition talks in 2021 at a reported Instacart valuation of $40 billion to $50 billion, but those discussions collapsed partly over regulatory concerns.

The latest talks remain ongoing, and a deal is not guaranteed.
